parole.significato: A game played with a shuttlecock and rackets (properly battledore and shuttlecock); a forerunner of badminton.
parole.testo: From Middle English batildore, batylledore, batildure, batyldoure, batyndore, probably as a blend of Middle English betel (“bat, club”) and Old Occitan batedor (“beater, bat”).
Calque of Old Occitan far amor, Middle French faire l'amour.
Inherited from Middle English mokadour, from Old Occitan mocador. For the development of excrescent /n/, compare harbinger, passenger.

parole.significato: A muscat grape or raisin, especially one from southern Spain.
parole.testo: From Middle English muskadel, from Old Occitan muscadel, originally a diminutive of muscat.

parole.significato: A type of Occitan lyric poetry in which a knight meets a shepherdess.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Old Occitan pastorela (“little shepherdess”), from pastor (“shepherd”) + -ela (feminine diminutive suffix). Compare etymology 1.

parole.significato: An itinerant composer and performer of songs in medieval Europe; a jongleur or travelling minstrel.
parole.testo: From Old Occitan trobar (“to find”) via Old French troubadour. Piecewise doublet of trouveur.
From Middle French thon + -y, from Old Occitan ton, from Latin thunnus, from Ancient Greek θύννος (thúnnos).

parole.significato: A closely woven fabric (originally of silk, now also of cotton or man-made fibres) with a thick short pile on one side.
parole.testo: From Middle English velvet, velwet, veluet, from Old Occitan veluet, from Vulgar Latin *villutittus, diminutive of villūtus, from Latin villus (“shaggy hair, tuft of hair”). Cognate with French velours.

parole.testo: Borrowed into Middle English from either Old French cabestan, from Old Occitan cabestan, from cabestre (“pulley cord”) or from Spanish cabestran, both of which derive from Latin capistrum (“halter”), from capiō (“take hold of”).

parole.significato: An adjustable loop of rope, such as the one placed around the neck in hangings, or the one at the end of a lasso.
parole.testo: From Middle English nose (“noose, loop”), of unclear origin. Possibly from Old French nos or Old Occitan nous, nos, nominative singular or accusative plural of nou (“knot”), with a required change in meaning shifting from the "knot" itself to the "loop" created by the knot. parole.significato: A long, strong stake, one end of which is set firmly in the ground, and the other sharpened.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French palissade, from Old French, from Old Occitan palissada, from palissa (“stake”), probably from pal (“stake”), or possibly from Gallo-Romance *pālīcea, from Latin pālus (“stake”) + -ade.

parole.significato: A paved outside area, adjoining a house, used for dining or recreation.
parole.testo: From Spanish patio, either from Old Occitan patu or pati (compare Occitan and Catalan pati), of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: A framework on a post, with holes for the hands and head, used as a means of punishment and humiliation.
parole.testo: From Middle English pilory, pillorie, from Old French pilori, pellori, which is either from Old Occitan espilori or Latin pīla (“pillar”).
